title: What Pastoral Care Actually Looks Like
subtitle: A working pastor on the unglamorous heart of shepherding people, the ministry of presence, and the daily labor of caring for a congregation

sections.title: Not the Stage. The Hallway.
sections.body:
Ask a young man why he wants to be a pastor and he will describe a stage. The lights, the open Bible, the sentence that lands and the room that goes still. That is the picture in his head, and it is not a sin to have it. But it is not the work.

The work is the hallway. The phone call you did not want. The hospital parking garage at an hour when no one is awake.

Pastoral care is what happens in the spaces no one applauds. It is the long obedience of being available to people who are not at their best, on days that are not their best, in places that smell like antiseptic and fear. I have preached sermons I was proud of and forgotten them by Friday. I have not forgotten a single one of the kitchen tables I sat at while a marriage came apart. The sermon is the part they see. The care is the part that makes the sermon true.

sections.title: What the Word Means
sections.body:
Pastoral care is the labor of helping a particular person bear a particular burden in the presence of God. That is the whole of it. Not a program. Not a department with a budget. A shepherd, knowing his sheep by name, going after the one.

The Bible never gives us care in the abstract. It gives us a man on the ground, a woman at a well, a child lifted off a deathbed.

So care is always concrete. It is this widow, this week, with this fear about the bill she cannot pay. It is the teenager who stopped coming and the reason he stopped that no one has asked about. The temptation in ministry is to love the congregation, which costs nothing, instead of loving the people in it, which costs everything. A congregation is an idea. A person is an interruption. Care begins the moment you let yourself be interrupted.

sections.title: Mostly You Just Show Up
sections.body:
Most of pastoral care is not advice. It is presence. It is the decision to be in the room when there is nothing to be done in the room.

We overestimate our words and underestimate our bodies. A grieving man will not remember what you said. He will remember that you came.

I have sat beside hospital beds and said almost nothing for an hour, and been thanked for it as though I had performed surgery. Because I had done the one thing that mattered. I had not left. The ministry of presence is harder than the ministry of words, because words let you control the encounter and presence does not. You sit in the discomfort. You let the silence be long. You resist the urge to fix what cannot be fixed and fill what should not be filled. Job's friends were never more useful than in the seven days they sat with him and said nothing. They became fools the moment they opened their mouths.

sections.title: You Cannot Care for Strangers
sections.body:
You cannot shepherd people you do not know. This is the part of care that has no shortcut and no scaling. It is years of small conversations, names remembered, families learned, histories carried in your head until they live there.

The pastor who only appears in crisis is a stranger arriving at the worst possible moment. The pastor who is already known walks into the crisis as a friend.

So you go to the recitals and the ball games. You learn which member buried a child a decade ago and goes quiet every spring. You remember that the man in the third row lost his job and has been too proud to say it. None of this shows up in a report. All of it is the substance of the work. Care is not an event you arrive at. It is a relationship you have been building so that when the event comes, you are not a clipboard and a collar. You are someone they trust to be in the room.

sections.title: What It Costs the One Who Gives It
sections.body:
Care takes something out of you, and anyone who tells you otherwise has not done it long. You carry other people's grief home. It sits at your own kitchen table. It wakes you up.

This is not a sign you are doing it wrong. It is the sign you are doing it at all. A shepherd who feels nothing has stopped shepherding and started managing.

But you cannot pour from a self you never refill. So the pastor who would care for others must let himself be cared for, must have a few people who know the cost he is paying, must go to God not as a professional handling holy things but as a man who needs the same mercy he hands out all week. I have failed this more than I have kept it. I have given the congregation a tenderness I withheld from my own sons, and called it faithfulness. It was not. Pastoral care that leaves your own house starving is not the real thing. The real thing begins at home and travels out from there, and never the reverse.
